metadata.title: On weight initialization in deep neural networks

nodes.name: Weight initialization problem (variance preservation across layers)
nodes.statement: If the weights in a neural network are initialized using samples from a normal distribution, ${\cal{N}}(0,v^{2})$, how should $v^{2}$ be chosen to ensure that the variance of the outputs from the different layers are approximately the same?
nodes.statement_short: Choose the variance $v^2$ of normally initialized weights so that every layer's outputs have roughly the same variance.

nodes.name: Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: The first systematic analysis of this problem was conducted by Glorot and Bengio \cite{glorot2010understanding} who showed that for a linear activation function, the optimal value of $v^{2} = 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer.
nodes.statement_short: For linear activations the optimal weight variance is $v^2 = 1/N$ (Xavier initialization).
conclusions: the optimal value of $v^{2} = 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer

nodes.name: He initialization
nodes.statement: In an important follow up paper, He and colleagues \cite{he2015delving} argue that the {\it{Xavier initialization}} does not work well with the RELU activation function, and instead propose an initialization of $v^{2} = 2/N$ (commonly referred to as the {\it{He initialization}}).
nodes.statement_short: With RELU activations Xavier initialization performs poorly; He et al. propose $v^2 = 2/N$ instead.
conclusions: the {\it{Xavier initialization}} does not work well with the RELU activation function
propose an initialization of $v^{2} = 2/N$

nodes.name: 30 layer network: converges with He but not Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: In support of their initialization, they provide an example of a 30 layer neural network which converges with the {\it{He initialization}}, but not under the {\it{Xavier initialization}}.
nodes.statement_short: He et al.'s 30-layer RELU network converges under He initialization but not under Xavier.

nodes.name: Why He initialization converges where Xavier does not
nodes.statement: To the best of my knowledge, the precise reason for the convergence of one method and the non-convergence of the other is not fully understood.
nodes.statement_short: The precise reason why the 30-layer network converges under He but not Xavier initialization is not understood.

nodes.name: Deep neural network layer recursions
nodes.statement: Consider a deep neural network with $M$ layers. The relationship between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer ($x_{m}$) and $m+1^{th}$ layer ($x_{m+1}$) are described by the recursions \be y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij} \enum{in1} \ee and \be x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{g}(y_{m}(i)). \enum{in2} \ee Here $p_{j} = {\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)$, ${\bf{W}}_{m}$ is a matrix of weights for the $m^{th}$ layer, $g$ is the non-linear activation function, and $N$ is the number of nodes in the hidden layers respectively.
nodes.statement_short: An $M$-layer network with pre-activation $y_m(i)=\sum_j W_m(i,j)x_m(j)$ and next-layer input $x_{m+1}(i)=g(y_m(i))$, $N$ nodes per hidden layer.

nodes.name: Distributional assumptions on weights and first-layer inputs
nodes.statement: The weights ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ are assumed to be independent identically distributed normal random variables with mean 0 and variance $v^{2}$. Consistent with the assumptions in \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving}, I assume that the inputs to the first layer are independent and identically distributed random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.
nodes.statement_short: Weights are i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,v^2)$ and first-layer inputs are i.i.d. with mean 0 and variance 1.

nodes.name: Mean and variance notation $r_m$, $u_m^2$ for $y_m(i)$
nodes.statement: For convenience, I use $r_{m}$ and $u_{m}^{2}$ to denote the mean and variance of $y_{m}(i)$ respectively.

nodes.name: Symmetry of layer-input moments during the first forward pass
nodes.statement: Due to the symmetry in the problem, all inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer will have the same means and variances during the first forward pass (i.e., $E(x_{m}(i)) = \mu_m$ and $Var(x_{m}(i)) = s_{m}^{2}$ for all $i$); the covariances between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer need not be 0.
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry all inputs to layer $m$ share mean $\mu_m$ and variance $s_m^2$ in the first forward pass, though they may be correlated.
assumptions: Due to the symmetry in the problem
conclusions: all inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer will have the same means and variances
the covariances between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer need not be 0

nodes.name: Variance-preservation goal: choose $v^2$ with $s_1^2 \approx \dots \approx s_M^2 = 1$
nodes.statement: The goal is to find the value of $v^{2}$ which ensures that $s_{1}^{2} \approx s_{2}^{2} ...\approx s_{M}^{2} = 1$ during the first forward pass.
nodes.statement_short: Find $v^2$ such that the input variances $s_m^2$ stay approximately 1 across all layers in the first forward pass.

nodes.name: Proposition 1 (independence of weights and layer inputs)
nodes.statement: During the first iteration, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$
nodes.statement_short: In the first iteration the layer-$m$ weights are independent of the layer-$m$ inputs.
conclusions: $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in \eref{in1} and \eref{in2}, $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer. Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$. Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$
nodes.statement_short: Express $x_m(k)$ as a function of earlier weights and inputs, which are independent of the layer-$m$ weights.

nodes.name: Express $x_m(k)$ via earlier layers
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in \eref{in1} and \eref{in2}, $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer.
nodes.statement_short: Write $x_m(k)$ as a non-linear function of the first $m-1$ layers' weights and the first-layer inputs.

nodes.name: Independence of $W_m$ from that function
nodes.statement: Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Layer-$m$ weights are independent of everything $x_m(k)$ depends on, hence of $x_m(k)$.

nodes.name: Extend to products $x_m(k)x_m(l)$
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$
nodes.statement_short: Conclude independence from products of inputs as well.

nodes.name: Mean of $y_m(i)$ is zero (in201)
nodes.statement: r_{m} = E(y_{m}(i)) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E(x_{m}(j)) = 0. \enum{in201}
nodes.statement_short: $r_m = E(y_m(i)) = 0$ since weights have mean zero and are independent of the inputs.

nodes.name: Expansion of $u_m^2$ into diagonal and cross terms (in203)
nodes.statement: \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= E\left(\sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right)^{2} \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) + 2\sum E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right). \\ \enum{in203} \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Second moment of $y_m(i)$ expanded into squared terms and cross terms.

nodes.name: Cross terms vanish (in2041)
nodes.statement_short: The cross expectation factorizes by Proposition 1 and vanishes because $E(W)=0$.

nodes.name: Derivation of the mean and variance of $y_m(i)$
nodes.statement: Taking expectations in \eref{in1} and using proposition 1, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0$ yields \be r_{m} = E(y_{m}(i)) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E(x_{m}(j)) = 0. \enum{in201} \ee Therefore, $u_{m}^{2} = Var(y_{m}(i)) = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right) - \left(E(y_{m}(i))\right)^{2} = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right)$. Using \eref{in1}, \be \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= E\left(\sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right)^{2} \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) + 2\sum E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right). \\ \enum{in203} \end{split} \ee From proposition 1, ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ and ${\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)$ will (a) be independent of each other, and (b) be independent of $x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)$. Using these results, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0 $ gives \newline \be E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right) = E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E({\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l))E(x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)) = 0. \enum{in2041} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Take expectations in the recursion, expand the second moment, and kill the cross terms using Proposition 1.

nodes.name: Mean of $y_m(i)$
nodes.statement: Taking expectations in \eref{in1} and using proposition 1, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0$ yields \be r_{m} = E(y_{m}(i)) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E(x_{m}(j)) = 0. \enum{in201} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Take expectations in (in1); mean-zero weights give $r_m = 0$.

nodes.name: Expand the second moment
nodes.statement: Therefore, $u_{m}^{2} = Var(y_{m}(i)) = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right) - \left(E(y_{m}(i))\right)^{2} = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right)$. Using \eref{in1}, \be \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= E\left(\sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right)^{2} \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) + 2\sum E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right). \\ \enum{in203} \end{split} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Since $r_m=0$, $u_m^2 = E(y_m(i)^2)$; expand the square into diagonal and cross terms.

nodes.name: Cross terms vanish by Proposition 1
nodes.statement: From proposition 1, ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ and ${\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)$ will (a) be independent of each other, and (b) be independent of $x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)$. Using these results, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0 $ gives \newline \be E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right) = E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E({\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l))E(x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)) = 0. \enum{in2041} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 1 and $E(W)=0$ to show each cross expectation is zero.

nodes.name: Variance of $y_m(i)$: $u_m^2 = Nv^2(s_m^2+\mu_m^2)$
nodes.statement: Plugging \eref{in2041} into \eref{in203} gives \be \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= Nv^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ \enum{in204} \end{split} \ee for all $i$. Interestingly, this result holds for any arbitrary covariance structure of the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer.
nodes.statement_short: The pre-activation variance is $u_m^2 = N v^2 (s_m^2 + \mu_m^2)$ for all $i$, regardless of input covariances.
assumptions: The weights ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ are assumed to be independent identically distributed normal random variables with mean 0 and variance $v^{2}$
conclusions: u_{m}^{2} &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= Nv^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2})
for all $i$
this result holds for any arbitrary covariance structure of the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer

nodes.name: Large hidden layer ($N$ large)
nodes.statement: To answer this question, I make the additional assumption that the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'; this assumption is reasonable given that most neural networks have several hundred nodes in the hidden layers.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the number of hidden nodes $N$ is large.

nodes.name: Proposition 2 (approximate normality of $y_m(i)$)
nodes.statement: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$.
nodes.statement_short: For large $N$, each pre-activation $y_m(i)$ is approximately normal.
assumptions: the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'
conclusions: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$.

nodes.name: Central Limit Theorem
nodes.statement: by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}.
nodes.statement_short: A sum of many i.i.d. terms converges to a normal distribution.
assumptions: $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables
conclusions: $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right) = 0$. Furthermore, for $j \neq k$, \be \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \ee where the last equality follows from \eref{in2041}. This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}. Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}). Thus, $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations.
nodes.statement_short: Show the summands $p_{ij}$ are mean-zero and uncorrelated, then invoke the Central Limit Theorem.

nodes.name: Mean of the summands
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $E(p_{ij}) = 0$.

nodes.name: Summands are uncorrelated, hence treated as i.i.d.
nodes.statement: Furthermore, for $j \neq k$, \be \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \ee where the last equality follows from \eref{in2041}. This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables.
nodes.statement_short: Covariance of $p_{ij},p_{ik}$ vanishes by (in2041), so the summands are taken as i.i.d.

nodes.name: Apply the Central Limit Theorem
nodes.statement: Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the CLT to the sum $y_m(i)=\sum_j p_{ij}$.

nodes.name: Weak conditions and conclusion
nodes.statement: Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}). Thus, $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations.
nodes.statement_short: Note the CLT conditions are weak even without i.i.d., so approximate normality holds in most iterations.

nodes.name: First-order Taylor expansion of the activation (in205)
nodes.statement_short: Linearize $g$ about 0: $x_{m+1}(i) \approx g(0) + y_m g'(0)$.

nodes.name: Mean of next-layer input (in206)
nodes.statement: \mu_{m+1} = E(x_{m+1}(i)) \approx g(0). \enum{in206}

nodes.name: Layer means equal $g(0)$ (in2061)
nodes.statement: \mu_{j} = g(0) \mbox{ for all } j\geq 1 \enum{in2061}.

nodes.name: Derivation of the general initialization formula
nodes.statement: When $g(x)$ is differentiable at 0, we can perform a Taylor expansion in \eref{in2} about $E(y_{m}(i)) = 0$. Assuming that the higher order terms can be ignored, \be x_{m+1}(i) \approx g(0) + (y_{m} - 0)g'(0). \enum{in205} \ee Taking the expectation in \eref{in205} gives \be \mu_{m+1} = E(x_{m+1}(i)) \approx g(0). \enum{in206} \ee This equation suggests that the expected value of the inputs to the $(m+1)^{th}$ layer has little dependence on the moments of the inputs to the ${m}^{th}$ layer. Using this result recursively suggests that for all layers (barring the first), \be \mu_{j} = g(0) \mbox{ for all } j\geq 1 \enum{in2061}. \ee Using \eref{in204} and \eref{in2061}, the variance of $x_{m+1}(i)$ can be computed from \eref{in205} as \be \begin{split} s_{m+1}^{2} = Var(x_{m+1}(i)) &\approx (g'(0))^{2} Var(y_{m}(i)) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + g(0)^{2}) . \enum{in207} \end{split} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Taylor-expand $g$ about 0, drop higher-order terms, and propagate the mean and variance through one layer.

nodes.name: Taylor expansion about 0
nodes.statement: When $g(x)$ is differentiable at 0, we can perform a Taylor expansion in \eref{in2} about $E(y_{m}(i)) = 0$. Assuming that the higher order terms can be ignored, \be x_{m+1}(i) \approx g(0) + (y_{m} - 0)g'(0). \enum{in205} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Linearize the activation about $E(y_m(i))=0$, ignoring higher-order terms.

nodes.name: Propagate the mean
nodes.statement: Taking the expectation in \eref{in205} gives \be \mu_{m+1} = E(x_{m+1}(i)) \approx g(0). \enum{in206} \ee This equation suggests that the expected value of the inputs to the $(m+1)^{th}$ layer has little dependence on the moments of the inputs to the ${m}^{th}$ layer. Using this result recursively suggests that for all layers (barring the first), \be \mu_{j} = g(0) \mbox{ for all } j\geq 1 \enum{in2061}. \ee
nodes.statement_short: Take expectations to get $\mu_{m+1}\approx g(0)$ and, recursively, $\mu_j = g(0)$ for all layers.

nodes.name: Propagate the variance
nodes.statement: Using \eref{in204} and \eref{in2061}, the variance of $x_{m+1}(i)$ can be computed from \eref{in205} as \be \begin{split} s_{m+1}^{2} = Var(x_{m+1}(i)) &\approx (g'(0))^{2} Var(y_{m}(i)) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + g(0)^{2}) . \enum{in207} \end{split} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Combine (in204) and (in2061) with the linearization to get the variance recursion.

nodes.name: General weight initialization for activation functions differentiable at 0
nodes.statement: Using the condition $s_{m}^{2} \approx s_{m-1}^{2} ... = s_{1}^{2} = 1$ along with \eref{in2061} and \eref{in207} gives \be v^{2} = \frac{1}{N(g'(0))^{2}(1+g(0)^{2})}, \enum{in208} \ee
nodes.statement_short: For any activation differentiable at 0, variance is preserved when $v^2 = 1/\big(N (g'(0))^2 (1+g(0)^2)\big)$.
assumptions: Assuming that the higher order terms can be ignored

nodes.name: Generality of the initialization formula
nodes.statement: Equation \eref{in208} provide a general weight initialization strategy for any arbitrary differentiable activation function. I use the results developed in this section to analyze the optimal value of $v^{2}$ for two commonly used differentiable activation functions - the hyperbolic tangent and the sigmoid.

nodes.name: Backward-pass constraint is not required
nodes.statement: In their calculations, \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving} impose an additional set of constraints to ensure that the variance is maintained even during the backward pass. I believe that this is not required, since the requirement that the variance of the inputs at each layer be the same ensures that the gradient flows through in the backward pass.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike Glorot–Bengio and He et al., no separate backward-pass variance constraint is imposed; equal forward variances suffice.

nodes.name: Hyperbolic tangent activation
nodes.statement: g(x) =\mbox{tanh}(x),

nodes.name: Xavier initialization recovered for the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement: we have $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$. Plugging these results in \eref{in208} yields \be v \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{tanh1} \ee which is precisely the {\it{Xavier Initialization}}.
nodes.statement_short: For tanh, $g(0)=0$, $g'(0)=1$ give $v \approx 1/\sqrt{N}$, i.e. the Xavier initialization.
conclusions: v \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}},
which is precisely the {\it{Xavier Initialization}}

nodes.name: Why deeper tanh layers are less saturated (Glorot–Bengio question)
nodes.statement: In their analysis of a neural network with the hyperbolic tangent activations, \cite{glorot2010understanding} find that the deeper layers in the neural network have a greater proportion of unsaturated nodes than the shallower layers. As is stated in their paper, `why this is happening remains to be understood'.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Glorot and Bengio observed deeper tanh layers have more unsaturated nodes and left the reason unexplained.

nodes.name: Variance shrinks by 1/3 per layer under uniform initialization (seq1)
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Density of the tanh transformation of a normal random variable
nodes.statement: $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{tanh}(y_{m}(i))$ will have a probability density function (pdf) given by \be f(y) = \frac{1}{1-y^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi u_{m}^{2}}}\mbox{e}^{\left({-\frac{t_{y}^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}\right)} \enum{tanh1}, \ee where \be t_{y} = \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right). \ee
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: The pdf of $\tanh$ of a $\mathcal{N}(0,u_m^2)$ variable is $f(y)=\frac{1}{1-y^2}\phi_{u_m}(t_y)$ with $t_y=\tfrac12\ln\frac{1+y}{1-y}$.
conclusions: t_{y} = \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right).

nodes.name: Shape of the tanh-transformed normal density
nodes.statement: we expect the activations to be (a) approximately normally distributed when $u_{m}$ is close to 0 and (b) bimodally distributed with local maximas near -1 and +1 when $u_{m}$ is close to 1.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: tanh of a normal variable is near-normal for small $u_m$ and bimodal near $\pm1$ for $u_m$ near 1.
conclusions: approximately normally distributed when $u_{m}$ is close to 0
bimodally distributed with local maximas near -1 and +1 when $u_{m}$ is close to 1

nodes.name: Explanation of sequential saturation
nodes.statement: To explain their finding, I begin by noting that in \cite{glorot2010understanding}, the authors initialize the weights using samples from a uniform distribution $\left(U[-1/\sqrt{N},1/\sqrt{N}]\right)$ having a variance of $1/3N$. Therefore, from \eref{in2061} and \eref{in207}, with $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$, we have $\mu_{m} = 0$ and \be s_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{3}s_{m}^{2} < s_{m}^{2} \ee \enum{seq1} respectively. From \eref{in204}, this implies that $u_{m+1}^{2}<u_{m}^{2}$ for all $m$ (i.e., $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$). Furthermore from proposition 2, $y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. Therefore, $x_{m+1}(i)$ will be the tanh transformation of a normal random variable. Using results from \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{tanh}(y_{m}(i))$ will have a probability density function (pdf) given by \be f(y) = \frac{1}{1-y^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi u_{m}^{2}}}\mbox{e}^{\left({-\frac{t_{y}^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}\right)} \enum{tanh1}, \ee where \be t_{y} = \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right). \ee Plots of this pdf for different values of $u_{m}$ (provided in Figure \ref{fig:tanh}) produce trends similar to those observed by the simulation studies of \cite{glorot2010understanding} (figure 4 in their paper). A comparison of Figure \ref{fig:tanh} and figure 4 of \cite{glorot2010understanding} suggests that $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, as is expected.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Under Glorot–Bengio's uniform init the variance $u_m^2$ shrinks with depth; the tanh-of-normal pdf then becomes less bimodal in deeper layers.

nodes.name: CIFAR-10 experiment with a 10 layer sigmoid network
nodes.statement: To compare the initialization described in \eref{relur} with the {\it{Xavier initialization}}, I use a simple 10 layer neural network whose architecture is described in Figure \ref{fig:nnarch}. For my experiments, I use the CIFAR 10 dataset \cite{krizhevsky2009learning} comprising 60,000, $32 \times 32$ color images evenly split over 10 classes. The dataset comprises 50,000 training examples (which forms the training dataset in my analyses) and 10,000 test examples (which forms the validation dataset in my analyses).
nodes.statement_short: A 10-layer sigmoid network trained on CIFAR-10 (50k train / 10k validation) to compare the proposed initialization with Xavier.

nodes.name: Proposed sigmoid initialization converges where Xavier stalls
nodes.statement: First, I train the neural network with the {\it{Xavier initialization}} for 10 iterations and compute the top 5 accuracy on the validation dataset for each iteration. Next, I repeat the process using the initialization stated in \eref{relur}. A comparison of the validation accuracies for the 2 cases is provided in Figure \ref{fig:conv}, which shows that the convergence appears to stall with the {\it{Xavier initialization}}, but proceeds rapidly with the initialization proposed in \eref{relur}.
nodes.statement_short: On CIFAR-10, validation accuracy stalls under Xavier initialization but rises rapidly under $v\approx 3.6/\sqrt N$.

nodes.name: Derivation of the He initialization
nodes.statement: To proceed, I use proposition 2 and \eref{in201} which state that for the first iteration, $ y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. We are interested in in the mean and variance of $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{max}(0,y_{m}(i))$. The mean will be given by \be \mu_{m+1} = E(y_{m}(i){\bf{I}}(y_{m}(i)>0)) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{e}^{-t}dt = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. \enum{relu1} \ee Similarly, \be E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{1}{{u\sqrt{2\pi}}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2}. \enum{relu2} \ee Using \eref{relu1} and \eref{relu2}, \be s_{m+1}^{2} = E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) - \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2} - \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2\pi} \approx 0.34u_{m}^{2}. \enum{relu3} \ee For the variance to be maintained at each iteration, we require $s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 1$ which yields \be u_{m}^{2} \approx 3. \enum{relu301} \ee Plugging \eref{relu301} in \eref{relu1} yields $\mu_{m+1} \approx 0.7$. By the symmetry of the problem during the first iteration, we expect $\mu_{m+1} \approx \mu_{m} ... \approx \mu_{2} \approx 0.7$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute mean and variance of $\max(0,y)$ for normal $y$, impose unit variance to get $u_m^2\approx3$ and $\mu_m\approx0.7$.

nodes.name: Mean and second moment of the RELU output
nodes.statement: The mean will be given by \be \mu_{m+1} = E(y_{m}(i){\bf{I}}(y_{m}(i)>0)) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{e}^{-t}dt = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. \enum{relu1} \ee Similarly, \be E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{1}{{u\sqrt{2\pi}}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2}. \enum{relu2} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the half-normal to get $\mu_{m+1}=u_m/\sqrt{2\pi}$ and $E(x^2)=u_m^2/2$.

nodes.name: Variance of the RELU output

nodes.statement_short: Combine to get $s_{m+1}^2 \approx 0.34 u_m^2$.

nodes.name: Impose variance preservation

nodes.statement_short: Require $s_{m+1}^2\approx1$, giving $u_m^2\approx3$.

nodes.statement_short: Then $\mu_{m+1}\approx0.7$, and by symmetry all layer means are $\approx0.7$.

nodes.statement: To understand why this happens, I compute the central moments of $x_{m+1}$ in terms of the central moments of $x_{m}$ when $v^{2} = 1/N$. From \eref{in204} we have \be u_{m}^{2} = s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}. \enum{r01} \ee Plugging results from \eref{r01} into \eref{relu1} yields the recursion \be \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{2\pi}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \approx 0.16(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}). \enum{r02} \ee Similarly, plugging results from \eref{r01} and \eref{r02} in \eref{relu3} yields \be s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 0.34(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}). \enum{relu5} \ee

nodes.name: Why Xavier initialization fails for deep RELU networks
nodes.statement: Equation \eref{relu602} shows that the variance of the inputs to the deeper layers is exponentially smaller than the variance of the inputs to the shallower layer. Therefore, the deeper the neural network, the worse the performance of the {\it{Xavier Initialization}} will be. From \eref{relu602}, $s_{22}^{2} \approx 1.62 \times 10^{-7}$ and $s_{30}^{2} \approx 6.33 \times 10^{-10}$. Thus the variance in the input to the $30^{th}$ layer will be $(0.51)^{8} = 3 \times 10^{-3}$ times smaller than the variance to the $22^{nd}$ layer, and explains the possible reason why the 30 layer neural network described in \cite{he2015delving} converges, but the 22 layer neural network does not.

nodes.statement_short: Input variance decays like $(0.51)^{m}$, so the 30-layer network's inputs are $\sim 3\times10^{-3}$ times smaller than the 22-layer's, explaining the convergence difference.
